item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: Former Navy SEAL says New Jersey’s Islamophobia bill puts protected speech in the crosshairs
item.description: A former Navy SEAL and lawyer warns that New Jersey's Assembly Bill 1146 could function as a "backdoor blasphemy law" chilling public debate.
item.content:encoded:
A New Jersey proposal aimed at combating anti-Muslim discrimination could make Americans think twice before criticizing religious and political ideas, a lawyer and former Navy SEAL warned.

Bill Brown, a partner at Parlatore Law Group, told Fox News Digital that Assembly Bill 1146 contains language broad enough to discourage public debate, even though the legislation expressly preserves First Amendment rights.

"The mere threat of state scrutiny is a direct assault on public debate," Brown said.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

The proposal would establish a state definition of Islamophobia and require public officials and law enforcement officers to consider it when determining whether alleged discriminatory acts were motivated by anti-Muslim bias.

Brown argued that requiring officials to use a definition that includes harsh criticism and other speech could make people afraid to speak openly.

CHRISTIAN GROUPS AND PASTORS SAY NEW CALIFORNIA LGBT HATE SPEECH LAW IS DISGUISED AS INDOCTRINATION

"The First Amendment guarantees that no religion or theology is immune to criticism," he said.

Democratic Assemblyman Joe Danielsen sponsors the bill, which is co-sponsored by fellow Democrats Assemblywomen Verlina Reynolds-Jackson and Mitchelle Drulis and Assemblyman Roy Freiman. The legislation describes a uniform definition as a tool to help officials identify and investigate anti-Muslim crime, harassment and discrimination."

Fox News Digital made multiple attempts to contact Danielsen and all three co-sponsors for comment but did not receive a response.

Its definition includes "hatred or severe disparagement towards Muslim persons or their culture," as well as "rhetorical, violent, or physical anti-Muslim manifestations."

Other examples include pulling hijabs from Muslim women, discriminatory treatment and blaming Muslims collectively for wrongdoing committed by an individual or group.

CONNECTICUT BARS NATIVITY DISPLAY IN STATE CAPITOL BECAUSE IT'S 'RELIGIOUS,' LAWSUIT THREAT SAYS

The bill would create no standalone criminal offense for criticizing Islam. It directs officials to consider the definition when reviewing an alleged violation of an existing policy, law or regulation prohibiting discriminatory acts.

It also explicitly says nothing in the legislation should diminish or infringe on rights protected by the First Amendment or New Jersey’s Constitution.

AMERICA'S FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR EXPOSES A POLITICAL BLIND SPOT

Asked about that safeguard, Brown maintained that the prospect of scrutiny itself could discourage people from speaking, regardless of whether a case ultimately succeeds.

He also singled out a provision in the bill’s legislative findings that lists "anti-Islamism" among terms that may describe the same characteristics as Islamophobia. Brown argued that the wording risks blurring the distinction between prejudice against Muslim people and criticism of a political movement.

JONATHAN TURLEY: FRANCE'S FREE SPEECH CRACKDOWN SHOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN POLITICIANS DEFINE TRUTH

"Islamism is a distinct geopolitical movement," he said. "It’s not just a religious faith."

Brown described the proposal as a "backdoor blasphemy law," arguing that government should protect people’s rights while allowing their religious beliefs to face public scrutiny.

PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH'

The legislation excludes criticism of Muslim-majority countries comparable to criticism directed at other countries. Brown argued that criticism of religious and political ideology also needs protection.

Brown said his concerns are informed in part by his military service. He recalled responding to two suicide bombings in Iraq and said he remains committed to speaking out against jihadist ideology.

He also recalled studying Arabic at Rutgers after leaving the military, where Muslim American classmates helped him when he struggled with the language.

For Brown, the broader concern is whether Americans will feel free to challenge ideas they oppose.

"True diversity is diversity of thought," he said.

item.title: With Skubal signing, the New York Mets should have bought themselves the 2027 World Series title | Ian Miller
item.description: Major League Baseball fans feared the Dodgers would ruin the sport, but the Mets' 9-year, $450 million Tarik Skubal deal flips the script entirely.
item.content:encoded:
Cancel the 2027 Major League Baseball season. Why even bother playing the games? We don't need a World Series, just hand the trophy to the New York Mets right now.

Sounds a bit ridiculous, doesn't it? Except those exact phrases were repeatedly used ahead of the 2026 MLB season to describe the Los Angeles Dodgers. Because they signed Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz after winning the 2025 World Series over the Toronto Blue Jays.

Now though? The Dodgers are on the outside looking in, thanks to the Mets' stunning, 9-year, $450 million deal with superstar starting pitcher Tarik Skubal. Who we were told just a few months ago was going to bring about the end of baseball after being traded to those same Dodgers at the deadline.

METS, TARIK SKUBAL AGREE TO RECORD CONTRACT AS MLB LOCKOUT LOOMS OVER OFFSEASON

First, some background on Skubal. He just turned 30, meaning he'll play all of 2027 in his age-30 season. He's been one of the best handful of pitchers in baseball for the past four seasons, with ERAs under 2.80 in each. His command and consistency is second to none, with walk rates from 2023–2026 of 1.57 per nine innings, 1.64, 1.52, and 1.53. Hard to be more consistent than that.

He's been worth, per Fangraphs WAR calculations, 3.3 wins above replacement in 2023 in just 15 starts, 6.0 in 2024, 6.7 in 2025, and 5.2 in 2026, despite making only 26 starts. Skubal is a two-time Cy Young Award winner, and if you made a list of pitchers you'd want taking the ball in a postseason game, he'd be at or near the top, along with Jacob Misiorowski, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Chris Sale or Paul Skenes.

NEW STATEMENTS FROM ROB MANFRED, MLBPA, GUARANTEE BASEBALL IS SHUT DOWN INDEFINITELY IN TWO WEEKS

He was widely expected to get the largest free agency contract for a pitcher ever handed out, and that's exactly what he got from Mets owner Steve Cohen and a beleaguered front office. At least three other teams, the Dodgers, Blue Jays and San Diego Padres, met with Skubal. But only New York was willing to get to a whopping $50 million per year for the remainder of his career.

Now though, it's worth evaluating what this actually means, the fan reaction, and how this impacts New York's chances of winning their first World Series since 1986.

The short version? Fans don't seem to be bothered by the fact that the Mets have now guaranteed over $1.2 billion to just two players: Skubal and Juan Soto. Yes, there's been some complaining about big markets, but there's little of the wailing and gnashing of teeth that explode when the Dodgers make an acquisition or signing. The implication here is that fans don't care when bad teams try to improve, only good teams. An interesting sentiment.

What does it actually mean for baseball, for free agency, and for the Mets? Well, there's plenty to dig into. For baseball, it once again means that money is flowing into the sport at a record pace. The Mets do not have the Dodgers' television deal that's caused such misplaced consternation among fans. They are conclusively the second team in their media market, although New York obviously is not your average market, and they ranked No. 12 out of 30 teams in attendance in 2025.

In fact, they sold 1.3 million fewer tickets than the Dodgers and 600,000 fewer than the Padres.

So how are they raking in enough money to afford $1.2 billion on two players? On top of that, they have to pay the rest of the roster while also paying tens of millions for the luxury tax, scouting, research and development and so on.

Maybe, just maybe, there's more money coming into baseball teams than they're willing to let on. That might have raised some interesting possibilities, wouldn't it?

As for what it means for free agency, again, this is why the players don't want a salary cap. Clearly, teams can afford these types of contracts. Clearly, the interest is there for a pitcher with a lengthy and recent injury history to make $50 million per year. It's not the players' problem that some owners are cheap, or some are more concerned with increasing their franchise valuations or raking in another $50 million in profits, than they are with fielding a competitive baseball team. That's on the owners to figure out. So why should players take a massive cut in both total income and potential peak income, just to make ownership richer?

But what about competitive balance? Doesn't this, as the headline suggests, guarantee the Mets a championship? Shouldn't we just cancel the season now?

MILWAUKEE BREWERS BROKE BASEBALL ON THEIR WAY TO REMARKABLY DOMINANT WORLD SERIES RUN

Of course not. It's ridiculous to even suggest that it guarantees anything. Just as it was ridiculous to suggest that the Dodgers bought their title, or would ruin baseball by trading for Skubal in the first place. We just saw, with the Milwaukee Brewers, how postseason baseball actually works.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Dodgers entered October with arguably the greatest playoff rotation in modern memory. Skubal, Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. It was better than their rotation in 2024 or 2025, and significantly better than any that the competition brought to the postseason. How'd it work out for them?

Well, all four of those pitchers started the four games of the NLCS. And the Dodgers lost all four. Brewers' Robert Gasser (who is not a Cy Young contender), was one of the best pitchers in the postseason. Despite a woeful strikeout rate and thanks to incredible luck on balls put in play, Gasser had a 0.60 ERA in the playoffs. He gave up one run in over 15 innings. Skubal gave up three in 11 innings.

Aaron Ashby was the most valuable pitcher of the playoffs, with just five hits allowed in 18 innings, only three walks, literally zero runs, and 20 strikeouts. He was making $5.5 million, compared to Skubal's upcoming $50 million salary. Drew Rasmussen also earned $5.5 million and was brilliant over 28 playoff innings, with just a 2.20 ERA. Gavin Williams was dominant too, making $822,000. Should Skubal make 30 starts in 2027, he will take home $1.67 million per start. More than double Williams' yearly salary. And Williams outpitched him in October.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

This is the problem with fans trying to say you can "buy" a title. You cannot. Because the small sample sizes of playoff baseball mean that players like Williams, Rasmussen, Ashby and Gasser can outpitch Skubal, Yamamoto or Chris Sale over a few weeks' span. It's not even remotely surprising that it happens! In fact, it happens all the time during the regular season, though nobody notices, or cares.

Gasser, who nobody outside of Brewers fans or hardcore baseball diehards had even heard of, threw the best start by a left-handed pitcher in a World Series since Sandy Koufax. Skubal's never made the World Series. That's how baseball works.

For the Mets in particular, they're still not very good! They were 74-88 in 2026, and assuming Skubal puts up another Cy Young-caliber six WAR season, and all other things remain equal, they'd be an 80-win team in 2027. That's still bad. They were bad at everything in 2026. Here's how they ranked in some important statistical categories last season:

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Skubal will help some, but one player ain't fixing that mess. Even with spending as much or more than any team in baseball over the past five seasons. And over $400 million in commitments for next year. Lindor had the worst season of his career and is now 33 years old. Bichette made over $40 million to be a below-average hitter. Former top prospect Brett Baty has looked awful. A.J. Ewing was a below average hitter. Juan Soto missed time and while still outstanding, was far below his 2024 peaks. Carson Benge was the lone bright spot, but used some BABIP luck to boost his numbers.

Their rotation looks solid, but the back half is still shaky at best. And as usual, there's no depth. Devin Williams was mediocre, and Freddy Peralta and Clay Holmes are now free agents.

This is the problem fans ignore when talking about free agency; teams paying for players in their 30s are paying for the declining phase of their careers. Especially with pitchers, there's added injury risk, and the valuation of these contracts makes it, so there's little margin for error.

Even if the Mets were good, signing Skubal wouldn't guarantee anything. And that's what makes baseball so beautiful. It's unpredictable, always. New York might win 100 games, or it would be equally unsurprising if they lost 100. Skubal might win a Cy Young, or get booed off the mound in August.

That's baseball.

item.title: UCLA lost but viral Miss California crown wearing cheerleader Sharlize True Trujillo continues to win
item.description: UCLA Bruins cheerleader Sharlize True Trujillo stays in the spotlight after the Ann Arbor loss to Michigan, with her Miss California crown and viral video.
item.content:encoded:
UCLA's undefeated season came to an end in Ann Arbor this weekend when they lost to Michigan 18-16 in a triple overtime game. The Bruins dropped from the AP No. 4-ranked team in the country down to the No. 10-ranked team following the loss.

It's not the type of loss you want to have this time of year. You have to handle your business against your unranked opponents no matter who it is and where the game is played. They didn't do that.

Despite the loss, UCLA's Miss California crown-wearing cheerleader Sharlize True Trujillo hasn't lost the spotlight. She went viral a couple of weeks ago in an 18-second clip on social media alongside cheerleaders Hayleigh Liu and Quillan Cas.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Sharlize is the redhead who makes an appearance towards the end of the clip, which has now been viewed more than 30 million times.

Her resume as Miss California 2026 and as the Miss America third runner-up has kept the attention coming her way.

One of the more recent articles about her introduced her boyfriend. He's an actor by the name of Jackson Dollinger, reports the NY Post.

TCU'S MOST FAMOUS CHEERLEADER ON THE SIDELINE AS 'LANDMAN' FILMED DURING HORNED FROGS WIN

But that's not all the internet has dug up about her. Sharlize is more than a viral pageant-winning UCLA cheerleader. She comes from a family of cheerleaders and has an extensive highlight package of her own.

A highlight package that shows those couple of seconds of camera time weren't a fluke. Her sister, Shariah True Trujillo, is currently a Denver Broncos cheerleader.

Her mom, Shelly True, is a former Broncos cheerleader herself who has "3 Super Bowl wins under her belt," according to her dance academy's website.

She's also currently Denver's choreographer and assistant director for the cheerleading squad. That's just a taste of mom's resume too.

That just goes to show that folks on social media have an eye for talent.

Sharlize True Trujillo was about as prepared as one can be when her viral moment came knocking. Congratulations to the entire family for helping out with that.

item.title: DK Metcalf avoids NFL and club suspension from the Pittsburgh Steelers following his ejection from Sunday game
item.description: DK Metcalf avoids an NFL suspension after his ejection vs. the Eagles, but a $6.5 million roster bonus and unguaranteed money cloud his Steelers future.
item.content:encoded:
DK Metcalf lost his composure but he didn't lose his ability to play for the Pittsburgh Steelers because the NFL has decided not to suspend the wide receiver despite him being ejected from Sunday's game against the Philadelphia Eagles.

The league has instead opted to review Metcalf's conduct during the game and decide if fines are in order, a source confirmed.

And the sound you hear coming from Western Pennsylvania is a sigh of relief.

DK METCALF DISQUALIFIED FROM STEELERS GAME FOR UNSPORTSMANLIKE PENALTIES INCLUDING TRYING TO POKE OPPONENT'S EYES

Earlier on Monday, Metcalf talked with Mike McCarthy, and the Steelers' coach said he was comfortable with the receiver's accountability and approach and indicated there would be no team discipline that is public.

So Metcalf is in the clear to continue playing.

NEW NFL FINE SCHEDULE IS GOING TO A POINT SYSTEM THAT COULD LEAD TO SUSPENSIONS BUT ALSO REFUNDS

Metcalf was ejected from the Eagles game because NFL rules stipulate any player flagged twice for unsportsmanlike conduct related to taunting, abusive conduct or striking another player, is automatically disqualified.

Sunday's disqualification marks the third time in Metcalf's career he is removed from a game. Metcalf has been suspended by the NFL previously, that coming last year when he got into an argument with a fan.

So what happened in this game that led to Metcalf getting ejected?

"I can't remember," Metcalf told reporters on Monday after leaving the locker room on Sunday without speaking. "I just wish I had been there for my team."

Metcalf didn't think himself responsible for what happened and, hey, that's possible because in football it is sometimes the reacting party that gets caught instead of the offending party.

So, yeah, that's what Metcalf is going with.

"You got to ask the people that seemingly do that to me," Metcalf said when asked about his temper issues on the field.

It is fair to say something set off Metcalf and that something almost definitely was personified by Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean.

RAMS OL ALARIC JACKSON EXPECTING TWO-GAME SUSPENSION AFTER PUNCHING BILLS DEFENDER BRADLEY CHUBB

The two players got into a fracas in the third quarter on a play in which Metcalf was blocking DeJean. The blocking turned into something else when Metcalf grabbed DeJean by the collar, DeJean grabbed back, one pushed the other and then other players surrounded the pair.

It was basically a routine football fight and that's when Metcalf picked up his first flag. On the next offensive series for the Steelers, Metcalf was caught on camera poking at DeJean's facemask.

"I mean, we were just competing," DeJean said. "Things like that happen in football. It wasn't anything crazy. Just two guys going at it. He was trying to block me, I was trying to get him off me. And it carried over to whatever that was at the end."

Metcalf said nothing happened at the end. He denied poking DeJean at all.

"I wasn't trying to poke him in the eye," Metcalf said. "I was just telling him."

None of this washes away the question of Metcalf's long term prospects with the Steelers.

He is turning 29 years old next month and has three years remaining on his contract after this season at a cost of $90 million. But all of that money is unsecured by guaranteed money.

The Steelers must pay Metcalf a $6.5 million roster bonus on March 13 to retain his rights. The club can decline to pay the bonus and move on from the volatile player, and while that will carry nearly $70 million in dead cap money through 2029, it also comes with a salary cap savings of around $54 million over that time.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

So Metcalf's future is not secured with the Steelers by his contract and its salary cap implications. But is he worth keeping based on his talent?

Well, that talent is undeniable. He's 6-4 and fast as the wind. He should be great and has been in the past.

But that was around 2020-2023 with the Seattle Seahawks. The numbers – yards, receptions, touchdowns – have been in steady decline since 2024, including the past two seasons with the Steelers.

Metcalf's production, in other words, exposes him to being released in the offseason.

item.title: $25 minimum wage backers frame midterms as 'blue-collar wave,' 'mandate' to raise pay
item.description: One Fair Wage's Saru Jayaraman says the midterms delivered a "blue-collar wave" and mandate for a $25 federal minimum wage to meet the cost of living.
item.content:encoded:
Democrats' huge wins in the 2026 midterms represent a "blue-collar wave" mandate for a $25 federal minimum wage, an advocate for the wage hike tells Fox News Digital.

One Fair Wage President Saru Jayaraman joined House Democrats and restaurant workers on Capitol Hill on Nov. 18 to urge the incoming 120th Congress "to answer the affordability election with a $25 living wage and to make the Living Wage for All Act a Day One priority."

"We're saying it's actually not a blue wave, it's a blue-collar wave. It's working people who didn't necessarily turn into Democrats but are demanding change so that they can meet the cost of living," Jayaraman said in an interview.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE ON MIDTERM WINS TO PUSH MASSIVE MINIMUM WAGE HIKES, BUT ECONOMISTS SEE TROUBLE AHEAD

"I don't care what their political affiliation [is], people are looking for help and change and relief because the cost of living is out of control," she added. "Nobody can live on the wages. Most people's pay doesn't meet the cost of living in America right now."

One Fair Wage co-leads the Living Wage for All coalition — a group of more than 100 organizations, including major teachers unions and progressive advocacy groups — pushing to more than triple the federal minimum wage, which has sat at $7.25 an hour since 2009.

SANDERS-AOC BACKED PROGRESSIVE DEBUTS FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE BILL WITH COALITION OF 100+ ORGANIZATIONS

Introduced in April by Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., and backed by 35 House cosponsors alongside a Senate companion from Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., the Living Wage for All Act would phase in a $25 hourly floor by 2031 for large employers and by 2038 for smaller businesses. The legislation would also eliminate the $2.13 federal subminimum wage for tipped workers and index future increases to the national median wage.

One of the bill's House co-leads is Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., a progressive who won an April special election before securing a full term on Nov. 3. Mejia, who was backed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has campaigned on progressive priorities including Medicare for All, a wealth tax and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

'CRAZY': MODERATES FEAR DEM LEADERSHIP PROMISED FAR-LEFT REPARATIONS AND ICE DEMANDS IN TURN OF VOTES

Small-business advocates and restaurant industry groups have repeatedly warned that steep federal wage mandates could force employers to cut staff, raise menu prices or close altogether — particularly in rural states with significantly lower living costs than major coastal cities.

Rep. Everton Blair Jr., D-Ga., who attended the Nov. 18 Capitol Hill press conference, dismissed arguments that a $25 floor would hurt lower-cost states, arguing the rate should serve as a nationwide baseline.

PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING

"We should be rallying around $25 at minimum, and it should be cost-adjusted for inflation, so that people can have a job that enables them to survive and thrive," Blair told Fox News Digital. He added that $25 an hour should be "the floor" and "should be higher in places with a higher cost of living."

While Blair acknowledged concerns that higher wage mandates could fuel inflation, he argued lawmakers must find a way to boost earnings while "keeping people afloat."

AOC-BACKED $25 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN SOUNDS GREAT — BUT AT WHAT COST?

The renewed push comes after Democrats swept into majorities in both the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms. However, when the new Congress convenes in January, Democrats will remain well short of the two-thirds supermajorities needed in each chamber to override a presidential veto — setting the stage for messaging bills aimed at forcing President Donald Trump to reject progressive economic proposals.

Still, Jayaraman insisted voters delivered an unmistakable verdict on wages as "people are overwhelmingly" demanding action quickly.

"There's a mandate from working people based on this election to deliver on raising wages closer to the cost of living," she said, adding, "Most people do not care about parties. Most people care about results. They want to see electeds deliver on the cost of living, and that means raising wages to the least you need to live anywhere in the U.S."

item.title: Bessent gave Iran weeks before it had ‘nothing left to trade.’ New sanctions expose what survived
item.description: Scott Bessent warned Iran had two weeks. Two months later, Treasury hit over two dozen entities in Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey moving billions for Tehran.
item.content:encoded:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned in September that Iran would have "nothing left to trade" within two weeks.

Nearly two months later, the Trump administration is still targeting the overseas financial networks Tehran has used to keep money moving despite sweeping U.S. sanctions in the midst of ongoing war.

On Monday, Treasury announced another round of sanctions targeting more than two dozen individuals and companies accused of helping Iran move billions of dollars through financial networks spanning Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey.

Bessent has repeatedly warned that Iran is nearing economic collapse, describing successive crackdowns as steps toward cutting off the regime's remaining financial lifelines. Yet each new round of sanctions has exposed more of the networks Tehran has used to keep doing business abroad — even as mounting economic pressure has failed to produce a diplomatic breakthrough.

COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES

While the administration says its blockade has largely stopped Iranian oil exports, Monday's sanctions detail how Tehran has relied on currency dealers, trading companies and middlemen to conduct business abroad.

Treasury identified approximately $14.7 billion in financial activity potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking between January 2025 and August 2026, underscoring the scale of the networks Washington is now targeting.

Just three days earlier, Treasury declared that Iran had exhausted its seaborne oil supply outside the U.S. blockade, saying no new oil had been loaded onto vessels since the launch of Operation Economic Outcast in August.

"The regime has exhausted its seaborne oil supply, and it may never see the revenue from the oil it has already sold. The ship is sinking," Bessent said Friday.

In a response to Fox News Digital, Treasury said Iran has not loaded a single barrel of oil onto vessels since Aug. 25, 2026, and claimed Tehran is struggling to access foreign currency and recover proceeds from previous oil sales.

The department also provided a report showing the Iranian rial has lost roughly 25% of its value since August, while inflation reached 90% in September. Treasury said it is continuing to target alternative financial channels, including cryptocurrency exchanges, as Tehran looks for ways around U.S. restrictions.

BESSENT SAYS IRAN WILL HAVE 'NOTHING LEFT TO TRADE' WITHIN TWO WEEKS AS OIL LIFELINE DRIES UP

But even as the administration claims success in cutting off new oil shipments, Treasury is still pursuing Iranian operatives accused of collecting billions of dollars from previous sales. Friday's sanctions targeted four individuals involved in recovering oil revenues held overseas, some of which Treasury said had been diverted by middlemen for personal gain.

Bessent's September prediction was hardly his first warning that Tehran was approaching an economic breaking point.

Months earlier, he said U.S. sanctions were "asphyxiating" Iran's economy and warned that the country could soon be forced to shut down oil wells as storage facilities filled up.

By late August, Bessent was predicting Iran's economy could collapse within "weeks or months," as the administration launched Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign aimed at cutting off the regime's remaining revenue.

The warnings continued in October, when Bessent projected Iran's economy could shrink by more than 25% over the year ending in March 2027. Earlier this month, he described the country as experiencing one of the fastest economic collapses in history.

BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY

The administration had increasingly turned to economic pressure after months of military strikes failed to force Tehran into an agreement. Washington reimposed its naval blockade in July after an interim deal collapsed, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in September that the price Iran would pay going forward would be primarily economic, although military action remained an option.

But neither the military campaign nor the mounting economic pressure has produced a broader agreement. Iran continues to demand sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and an end to the blockade, while Washington is pressing Tehran for concessions on its nuclear program and regional activities.

Despite months of escalating pressure, Treasury is still identifying overseas financial networks that have allowed Iran to conduct business outside traditional banking channels.

Iran has spent decades developing ways around American financial restrictions, relying on middlemen, shell companies and foreign currency exchanges to keep trade flowing even as Washington moves to cut off its access to international markets.

Monday's announcement detailed some of those channels, including exchange houses and trading companies operating across Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong.

Among the newly sanctioned entities was an Iranian currency exchange center that Treasury says facilitates tens of billions of dollars in annual trade, connecting exporters holding foreign currency with importers seeking to purchase goods abroad.

item.title: Russia warns of 'preventive nuclear attack' as Medvedev claims Ukraine, NATO crossed line
item.description: Dmitry Medvedev claims Ukraine and NATO have crossed thresholds that could make a preventive nuclear attack by Russia possible, warning Kyiv's allies.
item.content:encoded:
Russia warned Monday that it could carry out a "preventive nuclear attack" under certain circumstances, with former President Dmitry Medvedev claiming Ukraine and NATO allies have already crossed certain thresholds that could push Moscow to consider using nuclear weapons.

"The massive use of non-nuclear means that cause catastrophes makes a preventive nuclear attack by the Russian Federation possible," Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote in an article published Monday in the Moscow Journal of International Law and excerpted by the state news agency TASS.

Medvedev also warned that "secret or hidden supplies of nuclear weapons from the West to Kyiv will provoke a legitimate preventive nuclear attack by Russia."

MOSCOW THREATENS NUCLEAR RESPONSE OVER TINY FORTRESS WEDGED BETWEEN US ALLIES AS CLASH FEARS GROW

"Kyiv and its allies must remember that the Russian Federation not only has the right, but in various situations has the obligation to use nuclear weapons," he wrote.

Medvedev's warning came amid continuing tensions between Moscow and the West over the nearly five-year war in Ukraine and NATO's military support for Kyiv.

He argued that Ukraine and its Western allies have already created circumstances under which Russia could consider a nuclear strike, though he said Russian President Vladimir Putin carefully weighs the consequences before making such a decision.

"Formally, in a number of cases, the parties collectively opposing us (Ukraine, NATO countries, and several Western countries outside the alliance) have already created situations in which Russia considers the possibility of launching a nuclear strike," Medvedev wrote in the article, titled "State Sovereignty and Nuclear Weapons: International Legal Aspects of Ensuring National Security".

TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL

Despite those warnings, Medvedev wrote that Putin "is always guided by a comprehensive analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage inflicted and the retaliatory measures."

Medvedev also said Russia has not used nuclear weapons during the war with Ukraine because it has not considered them necessary, though he warned that calculation could change.

"Obviously, so far the course of events in the Ukrainian crisis has not created a state of direct necessity to use nuclear weapons," he wrote.

"The decision on Russia's use of nuclear weapons during the special military operation was not taken due to the lack of a direct necessity to do so," he added, using the Kremlin's preferred term for the war in Ukraine.

Medvedev argued that while Russia's nuclear doctrine does not explicitly authorize preventive nuclear strikes, certain scenarios — including catastrophic attacks using conventional weapons or the transfer of nuclear arms to Ukraine — could justify preemptive action. 

He said any final decision rests solely with Putin.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

"In making such decisions, the Russian president is always guided by a complete analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage caused and the retaliatory measures," Medvedev wrote.

"The Kyiv regime and its sponsors must not harbor dangerous illusions," he warned.

"If the scenarios mentioned above were to occur, the head of state not only has the right, but also the obligation to use nuclear weapons. All those who are currently fanning the flames must fully realize this".

Medvedev's remarks came within days of President Donald Trump meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Nov. 19 in Shenzhen, China, where the leaders of the three nuclear powers agreed to pursue talks aimed at reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

While the summit produced no major breakthrough on arms reductions, the leaders reaffirmed in a declaration that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.

TRUMP WILL FACE REPORTERS AFTER HISTORIC XI-PUTIN TALKS AS WAR QUESTIONS LINGER

To support his argument, Medvedev cited a 1996 International Court of Justice advisory opinion, contending that international law does not categorically prohibit the use of nuclear weapons when a state's survival is at stake.

The court concluded that the threat or use of nuclear weapons would generally violate international humanitarian law, but it did not definitively resolve whether such use would be lawful in extreme circumstances of self-defense.

Medvedev, who served as Russia's president from 2008 to 2012 and later as prime minister under Putin, has become one of Moscow's most outspoken voices on nuclear escalation since Russia invaded Ukraine.

Medvedev accused NATO members of undermining nonproliferation efforts, criticizing Germany's participation in nuclear deterrence arrangements and arguing that NATO's nuclear-sharing policies do not represent a universally accepted interpretation of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)

On Monday, he also accused the U.S. of applying double standards toward Iran and said Washington used nonproliferation fears to justify military action against Tehran while following its own objectives.

item.title: Dem lawmaker to resign after report says he made 'unwelcome' sexual advances toward staffer
item.description: The House Ethics Committee says Rep. Jimmy Gomez's advances toward a House staffer could implicate D.C. laws on criminal sexual assault, its report claims.
item.content:encoded:
A West Coast Democrat announced his resignation from the House of Representatives after their bipartisan internal watchdog stated that he could have committed criminal sexual assault against congressional staffers on multiple occasions.  

An explosive report by the House Ethics Committee released on Monday claimed that Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., violated congressional rules on sexual misconduct by making "unwelcome" advances toward a staffer for the House, disregarding the power imbalance between lawmakers and aides in the process. 

The report also went a step further, warning Gomez could have violated existing law.

Gomez has since announced his intent to resign on Dec. 1.

HOUSE DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATED OVER ALLEGED 'INAPPROPRIATE SEXUAL CONTACT' WITH STAFFER

The bipartisan panel found that "Representative Gomez knew or had reason to know that his contact was not welcome" when out with the staffer, called "Witness 1," at a D.C. bar.

"There is also evidence that he knew or had reason to know his repeated advance towards Witness 1 in his congressional office was inappropriate and unwelcome. Accordingly, Representative Gomez’s conduct towards Witness 1 could implicate D.C. laws related to criminal sexual assault, including misdemeanor sexual abuse," the report said.

SWALWELL ANNOUNCES RESIGNATION FROM CONGRESS AFTER SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS TORPEDOED GUBERNATORIAL BID

Gomez has not been charged with any crime and has maintained his innocence. Fox News Digital reached out to his office for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Gomez was a close ally of disgraced former Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., who resigned after being accused of sexual assault — which he denied. Gomez is also founder of the pro-family Congressional Dads Caucus.

The bipartisan ethics panel announced in August that it was investigating Gomez over allegations including "inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer."

Gomez told Fox News Digital at the time that he "made personal mistakes outside my marriage" but added that his extramarital relations were consensual and that he did not break any laws.

CAPITOL HILL SEX SCANDALS TRIGGER NEW PUSH TO REDRAW THE LINE FOR LAWMAKERS

But the lawyers for one of the women interviewed by the committee disputed that in comments to Fox News Digital, accusing the congressman of sexual assault.

Monday’s report shows the committee appears to support her side of the story, and that Gomez’s actions "at various junctures suggests he knew that what he was doing was wrong."

The staffer is identified as having worked for a congressional leadership office, rather than on Gomez’s own staff.

Before coming out with her accusations, the staffer testified to the committee that she did not want Gomez "to feel upset in any way," and that she was "afraid that I was going to get in trouble at work," the report said.

"Even if Representative Gomez believed that his actions were wholly consensual, his failure to appreciate the reality of this power dynamic and thus the untenable position he put a young congressional staffer in, is inconsistent with the standards required of a Member of Congress," the report said.

The investigation into Gomez began after reports surfaced that he had been seen kissing a congressional staffer at a party attended by lawmakers and House employees.

Gomez initially disclosed two relationships involving congressional staffers, describing one as a past consensual sexual relationship and the other as "one sole occasion" of "consensual kissing."

GOP LAWMAKER'S GIFTS, 'EFFUSIVE AFFECTION' TOWARD YOUNG STAFFERS DETAILED IN EXPLOSIVE ETHICS REPORT

However, investigators found credible allegations that Gomez made unwanted sexual advances more than once toward the second woman, Witness 1, which the woman claimed was "nonconsensual whatsoever."

The woman, who was in her mid-20s at the time, testified that Gomez put his hand underneath her skirt and penetrated her with his fingers without consent during a February 2024 gathering at a bar in D.C., and testified to investigators that she fled to the bathroom crying after the incident.

Gomez defended himself against the allegation, telling the committee that the woman "did not say no," and did not "push" him away, while denying penetrating her.

Investigators described a second encounter with the woman in July 2024, claiming that Gomez grabbed her as she attempted to leave his congressional office, pulled her toward him and tried to kiss her.

She described Gomez as "[p]retty forceful" and said she repeatedly tried to push him away, the report said.

Gomez denied the allegation, maintaining that he merely hugged the woman and kissed her on the cheek.

Investigators then refuted his defense after they examined text messages suggesting Gomez was concerned about being seen with the woman by members of his staff, noting that he switched their communications to Signal and enabled disappearing messages. The committee also noted that Gomez initially disclosed only consensual kissing before later acknowledging sexual contact during his testimony.

After reviewing documents and speaking with 10 witnesses, the committee concluded that Gomez violated clauses 1 and 18(b) of the House Code of Official Conduct, which prohibit unwelcome sexual advances toward House employees and require lawmakers to conduct themselves in a manner reflecting creditably on the House.

Investigators concluded that Gomez's conduct caused the woman significant emotional distress and contributed to her decision to leave congressional employment in 2025.

"The Committee reiterates its commitment to investigating allegations and providing accountability to those who face sexual misconduct from Members and their staff. Here, the House lost Witness 1 as a competent and able staffer because of Representative Gomez’s misconduct and because of a broader culture of disrespect and toxic sexual behavior toward staff that permeates life on the Hill and is long overdue for correction," the report said.

A slew of lawmakers on both sides have been accused of sexual assault or harassment over the last year, prompting a reckoning over how Congress protects staffers from predatory work environments.

item.title: California nursing student and mom arrested months after man’s body turns up in ravine: police
item.description: A truck driver's call near Livermore, California, led police to Marcelino Perez Jimenez's body in a ravine and a murder investigation reaching San Jose.
item.content:encoded:
A truck driver’s roadside stop near Livermore, California, led police to a man’s body in a ravine and, eventually, to a 22-year-old nursing student and her mother.

The driver called 911 on Aug. 25 after spotting what appeared to be a body below the road, KTVU FOX 2 reported.

Alameda County sheriff’s deputies found Marcelino Perez Jimenez who had been stabbed multiple times. San Jose police say they believe he was killed in an apartment where he was last seen three days earlier.

HIKER IN GEORGIA MAKES DISTURBING DISCOVERY ON MOUNTAIN

Jimenez had gone into the apartment with Alexia Nieves Solache on Aug. 22. She was carrying a 24-pack of beer, according to charging documents reviewed by The Mercury News.

The next day, security cameras at the complex allegedly caught Solache and her mother, Veronica Rangel, struggling to move a heavy box. The women used a hand truck to get it into a rental car, the documents said.

WIFE AND DAUGHTER ARRESTED AFTER DNA IDS MAN WHOSE SEVERED HEAD WAS FOUND IN TRASH BAG

Police say investigators traced a vehicle from the complex to the stretch of road near the ravine where Jimenez was found.

Police arrested Solache in Los Angeles on Oct. 27 and took Rangel, 55, into custody in San Jose the same day. Both were booked on suspicion of murder, police said.

MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PARTNER ARRESTED IN MEXICO NEARLY TWO YEARS AFTER FLEEING WITH THEIR TWO CHILDREN

Solache faces a murder charge, and Rangel is accused of helping conceal the crime, The Mercury News reported. Rangel was released under supervision and told the outlet she believes her daughter acted in self-defense.

How Solache and Jimenez knew each other remains unclear. Police say they are still investigating what led to the killing.

Fox News Digital reached out to the San Jose Police Department for comment.

item.title: NFL refs continue to be shockingly bad, Tom Jackson was our childhood & has fantasy football lost its luster?
item.description: Tom Jackson and Chris Berman's "NFL Primetime" defined Sunday nights before RedZone existed, and fans are mourning a piece of their childhood.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

We're here, folks ...

The most useless work week of the year ... every single year. It never fails. Seriously. Is there a more pointless "three-day" work week than the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday leading up to Thanksgiving?

Half the company is off all week. The remaining soldiers have already mentally checked out. And if they haven't checked out today, just wait till you see those Zoom meetings come Wednesday. If it's not canceled, it'll be the shortest meeting of the year. Trust me.

I'm fairly certain we wrapped our A.M. OutKick meeting this morning in about six minutes. Those things usually go about 20 minutes on a good day.

You can feel it in the air. The Monday of Thanksgiving week is always a good one. Morale is UP right now. The stock market is green (thanks, Jensen!). We've got a full week of FOOTBALL staring us right in our fat, American faces.

Who has it better than us today? Nobody. Let's roll.

NFL EXECS AND COACHES WANT LEAGUE TO REIN IN 'OUT OF CONTROL' OFFICIALS AND HOPE SUSPENSIONS SIGNAL A START

Welcome to a Monday Nightcaps — the one where the horrible NFL refs made a call so egregious yesterday, I'm honestly not sure we need to have instant replay anymore.

What's the point? Clearly, it doesn't work.

What else? I've got turkey tips from a few readers with the big day in just 72 hours, and I've got a legit question about fantasy football that pains to me ask, but I need to ask it.

I'm worried about it, folks. You'll see.

OK, grab you whatever you want on this penultimate Monday of November — pour it out for Tom Jackson — and settle in for a Monday 'Cap!

I'll be brief, but ... we can't start a new week of sports without mentioning Tom Jackson. That was tough yesterday, right? We grew up with Tom Jackson in our homes, every Sunday night.

Back before NFL RedZone was a thing. Back before the Sunday Ticket. Back before social media and streaming and phone alerts, we had Tom Jackson and Chris Berman delivering us all the highlights from an NFL Sunday.

And we needed them, because we only got two games a day most of the time. That was it. The internet took an hour to boot up if you wanted to check the other scores. There was no Twitter. There was no Scott Hanson.

NFL REFS HAVE SET ALL-TIME RECORD FOR FLAGS THIS SEASON, AND IT'S CHANGING THE OUTCOME OF GAMES

There was your two games on FOX and CBS, and Boomer and Tom Jackson at night.

And it was awesome:

I'd argue that NFL Primetime was the most important — most influential — show of my lifetime. I'm serious. The music. The chemistry between Boomer and Tom Jackson. The highlights. The anticipation as a kid of seeing how all the other games played out that afternoon.

They just don't make shows like that anymore, which makes sense. What good would it do? At this point, we all know the scores of any given game before the next commercial break. We literally have the ability to watch any game we want, and we can watch all of them at the same time.

NFL Primetime was RedZone and the Sunday Ticket before any of those things existed. It was perfect. Tom Jackson was incredible, and one of our crack OutKick editors — a former ESPNer — said he was an even better person off camera. What you saw on TV is what you got.

We lost a piece of our soul yesterday as sports fans. We lost a piece of our childhood.

Thanks for everything, Tom.

Well done by Boom. He doesn't have the fastball like he did back in the day, but every once in a while he can still reach back and find some velo. He nailed that moment.

OK, let's go from the studio to the actual field, and check in on another big NFL Sunday ...

Not a ton of great games yesterday — the schedule was brutal — but we did get a good one in Carolina, and plenty of drama in New York.

Shockingly (not at all), the refs once again made themselves part of the story. They just can't help themselves, can they? Every single week, it's something new.

This time? How about an absolutely ridiculous call on Parker Washington's apparent touchdown late in the game at MetLife:

Just a spectacularly bad call. Very rarely — and I mean VERY rarely — does the TV ref ever disagree with the call on the field. You just don't see it.

Gene Steratore, to his credit, was stunned at how bad that call was. I don't blame him. If we live in a world where THAT isn't a catch, I don't know what to do.

And I know I sound like a guy who had money on Parker Washington yesterday, but I actually didn't! It was one of the rare weeks where I didn't include him in some ridiculous six-player Anytime Touchdown parlay, and I'm glad I didn't, because I actually had one hit yesterday.

Amazing. What a feeling!

Anyway, that wasn't even the worst call of the day! Did you see what they let Mike Evans get away last night in Mexico?

What are we doing here? Come on. They didn't even really question the Evans one in real time! Did it ultimately impact that game? Probably not. The Niners smoked them.

But still, those two calls were just horrendous. I still can't believe, after all these years, we still don't know what a catch is in the NFL. It's really amazing.

OK, couple quickies on the way out. First? For those who still need turkey ideas for the big day, I have a couple emails in the chamber that you may like.

From Dom in Scottsdale:

Remember this basic fact of Turkey. The dark meat of the turkey, legs, thighs, wing, is finished at 180 degrees internal. (Get a quick read thermometer if you don't have one. It's a MUST have.) Breast is done at 160 degrees.

Cook the breast meat to 180 or above, you're going to need a lot of gravy. It will dry out, bigly.

Do whatever prep you do to prep the turkey, then about 20 min before you begin the cooking, place a 1 gallon freezer bag of ice cubes on top of the turkey. Right on the breast. That will bring the temp down on the breast, and allow you to finish both parts of the turkey at the correct internal temps at the same time. No overcooking one part and/or undercooking another...

It's money.

You learn something new every day in this class, folks. It's why we win (alleged) awards. Thanks, Dom!

Next? From Darren R:

This is the way I cooked the turkey, than actual prep. Stuff it with fruit; the fave seemed to be peaches, plums, citrus(1 or 2 lemons/limes), and some garlic. Use garlic powder and the highest smoke point oil you can get. Put it upside down 1st, then flip it, in a 500° oven. For a 12 pounder, 5 minutes, then 10. You will need fans and an open windows. It smokes, big time.

Pull it and drop the temp to 290/300. Roast it to 120-125° and pull it. It'll keep cooking while you do too. Say 30 minutes it'll be 160+. Incredibly juicy and fragrant, you can smell/taste the fruit. The fans are Important cause there is smoke. Easy, great, but smokey at first.

Holy cow! That method sounds like it's for the advanced class. I like the creativity, although I'd imagine if I were going to employ that method, I'd just use my smoker? Regardless, I do like stuffing it with fruit. Nice touch, Darren!

Finally, on the way out, I'll go ahead and leave the class with a question for the week as I usually do on Mondays ...

First of all, my question isn't actually about whether or not Parker Washington should have been awarded points for a touchdown he didn't score in a fantasy game. That's one of the dumbest things I've ever heard. Just an insane thing to do.

My question is this ...

Has fantasy football lost its luster? I've thought about this a lot this year. I used to love fantasy football. LOVE it. I would work the waiver wire and make trades all fall long. I'd spend hours trying to make my team better, and live and die with my players on Sundays.

Now? I just don't really care anymore. I still play, and I still enjoy it, but I don't care nearly as much as I did. The reason, I think, is fairly obvious ...

Sports gambling.

It's completely taken over, and usurped, fantasy football. That's certainly the case down here in Florida, where it's still fairly new. I'm far more interested in the players I gamble on than the players I draft for my fantasy team.

If my fantasy team loses, but I hit a $500 parlay, am I really that bummed? Nope.

Think about all the commercials you see on NFL Sundays now. They used to all about fantasy football. And then Daily Fantasy. And now? It's all sports betting.

Either that or ads for Skyrizi, Rinvoq, Dupixent or Tremfya. Take your pick!

Are you feeling the same way? Am I crazy? Let me know! Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

Now go have a big holiday week.

item.title: States rally behind Catholic church in first-of-its-kind Supreme Court fight over prayer shrine
item.description: A Kentucky Catholic community's Virgin Mary prayer grotto sparked a neighbors' zoning fight now at the Supreme Court in a RLUIPA religious liberty case.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A Catholic religious community's plans to build a small shrine to the Virgin Mary on its own property have triggered a years-long legal battle with two neighbors, drawing a coalition of state attorneys general into a potential landmark religious liberty showdown before the U.S. Supreme Court.

Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman is leading an 18-state coalition urging the justices to reverse a ruling that blocked the roughly 600-square-foot prayer grotto in Park Hills, Kentucky, despite the project initially receiving approval from local zoning officials.

The dispute pits the Missionaries of St. John the Baptist against neighboring property owners Joel and Elizabeth Frederic, who challenged the city's approval of the outdoor shrine and ultimately prevailed in Kentucky's appellate courts.

YOU SHOULDN’T NEED A PERMIT TO PRAY IN YOUR OWN HOME — THE SUPREME COURT SHOULD AGREE

"I’m proud to stand with other Attorney General colleagues from across the country in defense of these Kentuckians’ religious liberty," Coleman said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "This fundamental American freedom cannot be brushed away simply by a heckler’s veto, and I’m confident the justices will agree."

The coalition's intervention comes as the Supreme Court prepares to consider whether blocking a religious structure on an organization's property constitutes a "substantial burden" on religious exercise under the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA).

The case marks the first time the Supreme Court is considering the federal law's land-use protections, according to Coleman's office, raising the stakes for churches and religious organizations nationwide.

The controversy began in 2021 when the Missionaries sought permission to construct a 16-by-39-foot grotto honoring the Virgin Mary's apparition to Saint Bernadette in Lourdes, France.

SUPREME COURT SHOWDOWN LOOMS OVER ST MICHAEL STATUE BLOCKED FROM PUBLIC SAFETY BUILDING

The proposed structure would include a shrine, plaza, walking path and retaining wall, offering a quiet place for prayer and meditation.

The church building has stood on the property for nearly a century, predating Park Hills' zoning ordinance adopted in 1974, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting.

The Park Hills Board of Adjustment approved the project in April 2021. But the Frederics challenged the approval in court, arguing that the proposed construction violated local zoning requirements.

A trial court initially upheld the city's decision before the Kentucky Court of Appeals reversed, finding that the zoning board exceeded its authority in granting the necessary permits.

SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CATHOLIC PARISH'S CHALLENGE AFTER COLORADO BARRED SCHOOLS FROM UNIVERSAL PRE-K PROGRAM

The Kentucky Supreme Court affirmed the rejection of the Missionaries' federal religious land-use claim in December 2025.

Coleman previously defended the religious organization's position before Kentucky's highest court and led a 20-state effort in April urging the U.S. Supreme Court to take up the dispute.

The justices agreed in October to hear the case, with oral arguments scheduled for Jan. 20, 2027.

Ryan Gardner, senior counsel at First Liberty Institute, which represents the Missionaries, previously told Fox News Digital that the stakes extend far beyond the proposed Catholic shrine.

"This is a massive case for religious liberty because it has the potential to impact every single zoning law in this country," Gardner said in an October Fox News Digital exclusive.

Gardner compared the grotto's footprint to a swimming pool, underscoring the modest size of a project that has since reached the nation's highest court.

"RLUIPA is at the intersection of two very critical rights in this country: the rights of religious liberty and property rights," Gardner said.

Congress enacted RLUIPA in 2000 to protect religious institutions from certain burdens imposed through zoning and land-use regulations.

The Missionaries argue that preventing them from constructing a religious structure on their property substantially burdens their religious exercise.

The Frederics, however, have disputed that interpretation, arguing in their Supreme Court opposition brief that the religious organization failed to demonstrate why alternative locations for the grotto were unavailable.

They also challenged claims that lower courts are fundamentally divided over the legal standard for determining substantial burdens under RLUIPA.

The Supreme Court agreed to consider the substantial-burden question, rather than every issue raised in the underlying zoning dispute.

Kentucky Solicitor General Matt Kuhn, Principal Deputy Solicitor General Jack Heyburn and Deputy Solicitor General Jacob Abrahamson prepared the multistate brief, according to Coleman's office.

What began as a proposal for a quiet place to pray has become a national battle over religious liberty, property rights and how far neighbors can go in challenging religious construction on private property.

item.title: College basketball gets a new No. 1 as three teams fall out of the AP top five in a single week
item.description: Houston jumps from No. 8 to No. 1 in the AP Top 25 after winning the Players Era title in Las Vegas, earning a record 55 of 59 first-place votes.
item.content:encoded:
A week ago, seven teams sat ahead of Houston in the AP men’s college basketball poll. On Monday, only four voters could come up with one.

Houston jumped from No. 8 to No. 1 after beating Rutgers, top-ranked Florida and No. 11 Kansas in three days to win the Players Era 8 championship in Las Vegas. The Cougars earned 55 of 59 first-place votes and their seven-spot jump tied an AP poll record. The last team to go from eighth to first in a week was West Virginia in 1957, when Jerry West was playing for the Mountaineers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Florida had held the top spot since the preseason before Houston beat the Gators 86-76 in a rematch of the 2025 national championship game. The next night, the Cougars led Kansas 54-34 at halftime on their way to a 92-83 win.

Virginia picked up the other four first-place votes as the only member of last week’s top five to get through the week unbeaten. Michigan State and Duke, meanwhile, went from the top five to outside the top 10.

Houston deserved to be No. 1 and would’ve had my vote (if you’re listening, AP, I’d still like one of those). My question is why the Cougars had to jump all the way from eighth to get there.

Kelvin Sampson’s Cougars have earned a No. 1 or No. 2 seed in four straight NCAA Tournaments. And the analytics saw something in this Houston team that the voters apparently missed. KenPom had the Cougars third in the preseason, when the AP ranked them 10th, and still had them third heading into Las Vegas. Now the AP and KenPom agree on Houston. It just took the voters a little longer to get there.

Virginia moved up two spots to No. 2 after beating Old Dominion and Loyola Maryland. Florida landed at No. 3. Illinois jumped from No. 10 to No. 4. That puts the Illini one spot ahead of an undefeated Texas Tech team that beat them 84-78 less than two weeks ago.

What did Illinois do to get back in the voters’ good graces? Went into Cameron Indoor Stadium and beat Duke 99-78. Andrej Stojakovic scored 46 points, the most an opposing player has ever scored at Cameron. For comparison, Michigan State's entire team scored 46 points that same night in a loss against Tennessee.

What’s even crazier is that Stojakovic made 14 of his 21 shots. Michigan State went 9-for-50. One guy made five more baskets than the Spartans on 29 fewer shots. Sorry for that random aside, but I still can't believe a Tom Izzo-coached team could ever look that bad.

A week after climbing to No. 2 by beating Duke, Michigan State fell to No. 11, two spots behind the Vols. Duke took the biggest hit of anybody, dropping 11 spots to No. 16.

At least the Spartans stayed in the poll. Defending national champion Michigan dropped out after losing to unranked Villanova 79-73 in Philadelphia on Saturday, dropping the Wolverines to 3-2. Arkansas fell out after losing 81-76 to Indiana at Madison Square Garden. The Hoosiers followed that up by beating Kentucky and entered the poll at No. 23, one spot ahead of fellow newcomer Memphis.

Memphis was the first team out of last Monday’s poll, even after beating then-No. 10 Louisville by 20. The Tigers played once between ballots and won by 20 again, beating Evansville 82-62 on Sunday to improve to 4-1.

The voters were impressed enough with Memphis to put the Tigers at No. 24 this week. The computers aren’t impressed. Like, at all. KenPom has Memphis at No. 60. TeamRankings has the Tigers even lower at No. 72.

We can quibble about the teams at the bottom of the AP Top 25, but I'd rather take issue with how the voters handled UConn.

UCONN'S $32 MILLION-PLUS GAMPEL PAVILION NAMING DEAL LANDS IN COURT OVER A PROMISE MADE IN 1989

The Huskies played one game last week and lost 85-79 at Arizona. That cost them seven spots, from No. 3 to No. 10. Losing in Tucson to a very good Arizona team doesn't seem worthy of a major drop, especially when the same voters just moved Arizona up to No. 8.

KenPom actually moved UConn up from eighth to sixth over that same stretch and TeamRankings has UConn at No. 5.

When Houston beat Florida last Wednesday, UConn was the last unbeaten team from the preseason AP top five. About five hours later, Arizona handed the Huskies their first loss.

Last season, it took 33 days for all preseason top five teams to suffer defeat. Purdue, the preseason No. 1, started 8-0 before Iowa State went into Mackey Arena on Dec. 6 and beat the Boilermakers 81-58.

This year, all five had a loss just 16 days into the season.

Usually I can give you a short list of teams I think can win the national championship and feel pretty good about where I cut it off. This year? Houston is an easy pick for No. 1, but Arizona, Tennessee and UConn are sitting eighth, ninth and 10th. Would anyone be all that surprised to see one of those three cutting down the nets in April? And I'm not writing off Duke just because of two early-season losses, either.

Even teams outside the Top 10, like Vanderbilt, Kansas and Nebraska, are contenders to win it all this year. There's probably a surprise or two waiting outside the Top 25 that we don't even know about yet, too.

For all the talk about NIL ruining college sports, I think it’s helped spread the talent around in college basketball. It feels like more schools can put together a team good enough to win the whole thing. If that makes it a little harder for me to figure out who’s good before Thanksgiving, I can live with that.

Duke and UConn get to make their cases again Wednesday in Las Vegas, in a rematch of the Elite Eight game that ended Duke’s season in March. Still looks like a top-five matchup to me, even if the poll says it’s No. 10 UConn against No. 16 Duke.

And it’ll be interesting to see where voters think the loser belongs when next Monday rolls around.

item.title: Russia could launch nuclear-capable satellite within weeks, Western intelligence warns: report
item.description: Western intelligence reportedly warns Russia's nuclear satellite could launch in 60 days, threatening thousands of United States and allied satellites.
item.content:encoded:
Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit within less than 60 days according to new Western intelligence assessments reported Monday, raising fears that Moscow is preparing to deploy a weapon capable of crippling thousands of satellites used by the United States and its allies.

The intelligence reports emerged just four days after President Donald Trump met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a high-profile summit in Shenzhen, China, where nuclear arms control was a central topic.

The three leaders issued a joint declaration affirming that nuclear war should never be fought, but stopped short of announcing binding arms-control commitments.

NEXT GENERATION OPIR GEO: BUILDING AMERICA’S GATEWAY TO THE FUTURE OF SPACE-BASED MISSILE WARNING AND TRACKING

On Monday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz publicly addressed the reports, while the Kremlin dismissed the allegations.

According to a joint investigation published Nov. 23 by German broadcasters WDR and NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, Western intelligence agencies believe Russia has assembled a satellite known as "Sputnik-S," which has reportedly been stored in the Moscow region for several years.

Intelligence warnings shared among several NATO countries in early November indicated that the satellite, reportedly designed to carry a nuclear warhead, could be launched within 60 days. Germany's military Space Command reportedly assessed that a December launch was possible.

The German investigation also reported that military officials had briefed senior government figures, including German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, about the threat.

The reports prompted an immediate response from European leaders.

Speaking alongside Rutte in Berlin on Monday, Merz described the allegations as "shocking," while noting that concerns about Russia's nuclear space ambitions were not entirely new.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

Rutte, meanwhile, stressed that NATO was continually assessing its defensive capabilities.

"I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory," Rutte said, according to Reuters.

He added that the alliance's defense planning included threats in space and said NATO had response options that were not always visible to the public.

The Kremlin rejected the allegations. Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov questioned the credibility of the intelligence reports, saying they contained numerous unsubstantiated claims that were "hardly worth taking seriously," according to The Moscow Times.

"We haven’t seen the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that it’s certainly hardly worth taking them seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.

Russia's Embassy in Berlin separately dismissed the reporting as part of a propaganda campaign and maintained that Moscow's space activities were peaceful and consistent with international obligations.

The latest warnings follow an earlier assessment by the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency , which publicly identified Russia's development of a nuclear-capable satellite in October. "Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon," the DIA stated in its 2026 Challenges to Security in Space assessment.

NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK

As Fox News Digital reported on October 29, the agency warned that such a weapon could cause the rapid loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by governments and private companies.

Unlike a conventional anti-satellite weapon targeting an individual spacecraft, a nuclear detonation in orbit could potentially disable large numbers of satellites through radiation and electromagnetic effects.

The consequences could extend far beyond the military. Satellites support GPS navigation, international communications, financial transactions, weather forecasting and critical infrastructure.

The threat also has implications for Ukraine, whose military relies heavily on satellite communications, including SpaceX's Starlink network, during its war with Russia.

The concern was initially addressed on February 2024 when the Biden administration publicly acknowledged that Russia was developing a troubling anti-satellite capability, although officials said at the time that no such weapon had been deployed.

Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which prohibits stationing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in space.

The latest German reporting suggests the threat could be approaching a more immediate stage, but critical questions remain unanswered, including whether the satellite already carries a nuclear warhead and whether Western intelligence has independently verified the reported launch preparations.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, Pentagon, U.S. Space Command and German Embassy for comment.

After a months-long feud, the San Francisco 49ers have finally cut ties with embattled wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk.

The 49ers released Aiyuk on Monday following its blowout win over the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City, which ESPN first reported.

Aiyuk is now subject to waivers, but if and when he clears them, he would be an unrestricted free agent.

"We are looking forward to finding his next team," NFL agent Drew Rosenhaus said of Aiyuk, per ESPN.

This rift between Aiyuk and the 49ers got ugly at times, including the receiver posting numerous videos on social media to air out his grievances.

Aiyuk did return to the 49ers’ facility earlier this month, but he wasn’t very welcomed. Members of the Niners weren’t exactly thrilled he was there, and head coach Kyle Shanahan shared that sentiment when asked during a press conference.

SAN FRANCISCO 49ERS COACH SHUTS DOWN REUNION TALKS AS BRANDON AIYUK SEEKS NFL REINSTATEMENT

"I could care less," he said about a potential meeting with Aiyuk and 49ers brass.

"It’s been over for our football team for a long time," he said of the feud. "I don’t hear much except questions about it today. But it’s not too big of a deal for me to answer."

Meanwhile, Aiyuk said in a separate media availability that he’s "feeling great, feeling healthy."

"Long recovery process, long rehab process," he said, referencing his battle back from a torn ACL, MCL and meniscus suffered in his right knee during the 2024 season. He still has not touched an NFL field since then.

"I’m back to 100% and looking to get reinstated into the National Football League," he added.

Aiyuk was reinstated by the NFL, but remained under contract with the 49ers. Team GM John Lynch previously said he doesn’t expect Aiyuk to play for the 49ers ever again.

This came after he was placed on the reserve/left team list back in Dec. 2025 after he stopped showing up to the team facility for his rehab. And he’s been burning bridges within the organization ever since.

He had a contract standoff with team brass, an off-field reckless speeding citation and went scorched-earth on the organization through social media, where he called them "stupid" and accused Lynch of showing up uninvited to his home.

Aiyuk also mocked Shanahan’s demeanor and leadership, while tossing a thinly veiled jab at Shanahan’s serious car wreck in July, declaring, "You can’t win the race if you crash out."

Those social media posts also noted the Washington Commanders as a team he wished to go to one day. Aiyuk played at Arizona State with Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels, prior to the signal caller transferring to LSU, where he won a Heisman Trophy.

Now, the Commanders could possibly get Aiyuk on their practice squad and see where he’s at in terms of NFL readiness. Washington has lost Terry McLaurin, Jaylin Lane and River Cracraft for the season, and could use a receiver like Aiyuk, granted they want to take him in.

item.description: Democratic lawmakers call Elon Musk an "opportunist" and a "chameleon" after his MAGA remarks, warning of possible DOGE oversight probes in January.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic lawmakers are labeling Elon Musk an "opportunist" after the billionaire denied being "MAGA" last week and shared his regret for putting roughly $450 million toward the GOP in the midterm elections.

"I think that Mr. Musk is an opportunist," Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "I think he's a chameleon. I think he will be whatever benefits him and his business."

"It sounds like buyer's remorse to me," Rep. Christian Menefee, D-Texas, said. "Maybe he should spend his time focusing on his businesses instead of trying to buy politicians."

I SAW THE REAL DOGE FROM THE INSIDE. WHY THE MEDIA GOT DOGE AND ELON ALL WRONG

The political flip-flop callout comes after Musk made comments distancing himself from President Donald Trump and Republicans on Wednesday during The New York Times' DealBook Summit. Musk has put millions of dollars toward Trump, has previously campaigned with him and worked for the administration.

"Whatever," Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., said when asked about Musk’s comments. "That’s my response. Whatever."

Musk has also been facing wrath from Democratic lawmakers as a potential target of oversight investigations for his time as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

"You're the architect of DOGE," Carter continued. "You wreck people's lives. You tear people's opportunities and their careers apart in a reckless effort to so-called save money when nobody's pocket's been padded with his. If he really wants to do the right thing, demonstrate it, not in word, but in deed."

"I’m certain that he will be the subject of investigations," Rep. Sanford Bishop Jr., D-Ga., said. "We’ll deal with it when we deal with it."

An investigation into Musk and DOGE seems to be at the top of the list for many Democrats as the party pushes for investigations to look into alleged corruption under the Trump administration after the party took back majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections.

"I've not seen anything that he's done to reach out to Democrats or help or anything else in that regard," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., said when asked if Democrats would reach out to Musk to work together.

He continued, "What he's done is destroy the State Department [and] destroy diplomacy."

THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS

Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., urged Democrats to not make oversight investigations the center of their party’s agenda over the next two years with a majority in both the House and the Senate. He said the upcoming years should be focused on "leveraging this majority" to bring results to Americans.

"I think there will obviously be some degree of oversight into what happened with DOGE, and I think rightfully so," Figures said. "But I don't believe that sort of oversight can become the North Star of what the party is all about over the next two years."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who was just elected by his party to serve as speaker of the House, also recently left the door open to potential investigations into Musk when asked by Fox News Digital about the conversations surrounding oversight.
